title: Testing the Meshing Hypothesis in Prospective Teachers https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11251-024-09689-1
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 9, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton's page covers a study by Melzner and Kappes testing the meshing hypothesis, the popular claim that matching teaching methods to a student's preferred learning style improves outcomes, using a sample of 222 prospective teachers. Materials were presented either visually or verbally and matched or mismatched against each participant's stated learning-style preference, and the study found no significant learning-performance benefit from matching, regardless of presentation mode. The researchers also tested metacognitive measures like judgments of learning and confidence and again found no matching effect. Despite the null result, belief in learning styles remained widespread among the prospective teachers surveyed, and even directly teaching them about the lack of evidence produced only a slight, incomplete softening of those beliefs. Barton frames this as evidence that debunking learning-styles myths requires more than presenting contradictory data; it likely needs approaches built around conceptual change and critical reflection on existing beliefs.
points: There is no empirical evidence that matching teaching materials to a student's preferred learning style improves academic performance, even though students often express clear preferences.

Simply telling teachers the research contradicts learning-styles theory is not enough to change their beliefs — a large share of prospective teachers kept believing in it even after being shown the evidence.
Refutational texts and conceptual-change approaches that get teachers reflecting critically on their existing beliefs may be more effective than presenting data alone.
Using varied teaching materials and methods is still worthwhile, just not with the goal of matching them to individual learning styles.
quotes: This research article investigates the meshing hypothesis, which proposes that aligning teaching methods with students' learning styles improves learning outcomes.
A study of 222 prospective teachers found no significant evidence supporting this hypothesis, regardless of whether learning materials were presented visually or verbally.
Despite the lack of empirical support, the study confirmed the widespread belief in learning styles among prospective teachers.
Teachers should be aware that a significant percentage of educators and prospective teachers believe that teaching to learning styles is beneficial, despite the lack of evidence.
Teachers should prioritize the use of evidence-based teaching methods over learning style theories.
